entry.title: Goals Reached - Query, Search and Cite the Data
entry.content:
When Arslantepe went online last week, you could look at the data: one page per record, nicely linked. That was already one of my goals. But looking is only half of it. Linked Open Data is meant to be used. So in the last days, the website learned a lot of new things.

Ask your own questions

The new query editor lets you send SPARQL queries straight to the public triplestore. You don’t know where to start? There are example queries: the lead isotope ratios of a site, all finds of a type, the elements that were looked for but not detected, the arsenic contents of a phase, and a few more. Every one of them is tested automatically against the released data, so they won’t quietly break.

And a word on privacy, because it matters to me: the editor sends nothing before you press "Run", and it stores nothing. All its files come from this website.

Search

Not everyone wants to write SPARQL (I get it). So there’s now a search as well. It finds blog posts and records alike, and you can filter by kind of record or by topic. It runs completely in your browser, with an index built together with the site. No search engine in between.

Cite and download

Every record page now has a "Cite and download" section: a citation for that single record, and the record itself as Turtle or JSON-LD. On top of that:

  • the whole released dataset in one file,
  • a VoID description of it, so machines know what’s in there and where to query it,
  • a page on the data model, with a diagram of the records and the vocabularies they use,
  • and a data changelog on the Data overview: every release, with what changed.

And the IRIs themselves are getting smarter: ask https://lod-am.net/id/… for Turtle or JSON-LD instead of a web page, and you’ll get the data.

Seeing the data

The pages got some pictures, too. Every site page shows a relief map of the whole research area with the site on it. And the analyses of Hauptmann et al. 2002 now come with histograms of the element contents and lead isotope diagrams, drawn from the values exactly as reported. Oh, and there’s a light mode now, for those of you who read in daylight.

From release to website, automatically

Here the chain from the last two parts comes full circle. When a release goes live in the triplestore, it is sent to the website as a pull request. The website checks that the files are exactly the released ones, builds the pages and runs all its checks. Then it waits for me. I read what changed, write a line for the changelog, and merge. Minutes later, it’s online.

That’s the one step I want to keep by hand. The machines do the work; the decision to publish stays with me.

What’s next

More data! The machinery is in place, so the next publications are a question of checking the data, not of building tools. And a few last points in the automation workflow, of course. I’ll report back.

Curious for the code behind all this?

View LOD-AM/website on GitHub →

As always, if you have thoughts, suggestions, or you found something with the query editor I should know about, you know where to find me: info@lod-am.net or (if you have a GitHub account) in a comment below.

entry.title: Goals Reached - The Triplestore Goes Public
entry.content:
Remember the two old mini PCs under my desk? They’re still there, and they’re still doing their job quietly. But since today, one of them does something new: the LOD-AM triplestore answers SPARQL queries from everyone.

https://triple.lod-am.net/LOD-AM/sparql

No login, no API key. Just send a query. (Or, much easier, use the query editor on this website. More on that in the next part.)

Still Fuseki

I chose Apache Jena Fuseki back in June because it is real free software, and I haven’t regretted it. It now runs in Docker in a container of its own, Fuseki 6.2.0, and Watchtower keeps the image up to date.

What changed is how the data is organised inside. There are now two named graphs:

  • the knowledge graph: the vocabularies of LOD-AM, our typology, the topics of this blog,
  • the published data: the released publications from the pipeline.

A query without any graph sees both together. So you don’t have to care, unless you want to. And when one of them is updated, the other one stays untouched.

Open, but not too open

Making a database public on a home server needs some care. Reading is open to everyone. Writing is not: the endpoint that changes data needs the admin login, and the firewall only lets requests through that come from my reverse proxy. A query that runs too long is stopped after a while, so one heavy query can’t keep the little machine busy for the rest of the day. And there’s a small text index on the labels, so searching for a name is fast.

And because I care about privacy: Fuseki logs the queries it gets, but the logs are capped, so old entries disappear after a while. The privacy policy says what that means for you.

It updates itself

This is the part I’m proudest of, because it means I don’t have to log in to the server every time something changes.

  • When the pipeline has a new release, it tells the triplestore. The triplestore pulls the release, checks every file against the manifest, loads it in one go, rebuilds the text index and runs a smoke test. If anything fails on the way, the old data is put back.
  • Every morning, the triplestore looks at the knowledge graph on GitHub. If its data changed and all checks passed, it is loaded the same way.
  • If anything goes wrong, I get a mail. (I tested that, of course, by breaking it on purpose. It works.)

And once a release is live in the triplestore, it is handed on to the website. But that’s for the next part.

Curious for the setup? It’s all in the repository, minus the secrets:

View LOD-AM/triplestore on GitHub →

As always, if you have questions, suggestions, or you managed to write a query that brings my little server to its knees, you know where to find me: info@lod-am.net or (if you have a GitHub account) in a comment below.

entry.title: Goals Reached - From My Research Database to Linked Data
entry.content:
Here’s a question I avoided for a long time: where does the data for LOD-AM actually come from? The honest answer is: from my research database, which I newly started in spring. A relational database where I collect finds, contexts and analyses from the literature, one publication at a time. It’s my working tool, and it’s full of things that are not ready for the world: half-entered tables, open questions, notes to myself.

So I had a problem. I want the data out there as Linked Open Data. But not all of it, and not before I’ve checked it. The answer to that is the pipeline.

One rule: the database stays private

This was the first decision, and the easiest one. The database as a whole stays private. What goes online is a released publication: the finds and analyses of one article, and only what they point to (their sites, contexts, periods, types, laboratories). A publication is released when I say so, and not a minute earlier.

The same goes for the code: the pipeline lives on GitHub, but it runs on a container in my homelab, right next to the database. The data never goes to GitHub.

From tables to triples

In the Becoming Operational series, Arslantepe was converted by a script. That worked, but it meant that the rules of the data model lived twice: once in the conventions, once in the code. Now the way from the database to RDF is a mapping: R2RML, run with Ontop. The mapping says, table by table, which column becomes which triple. No hidden logic, no clever tricks in between.

The pipeline then goes through the same steps every time:

  1. take a snapshot of the database, so nothing changes while it runs,
  2. map it to RDF,
  3. enrich it with the details of the cited publications coming from a Zotero library
  4. check it: every term against the published ontologies, every record against the SHACL shapes of the knowledge graph,
  5. cut out the released publications, one file each.

If a check fails, nothing is released. That’s the whole point.

A release you can check

Every release comes with a manifest: which version of the pipeline and of the knowledge graph produced it, and a checksum for every file. That sounds boring, but it means that the triplestore and the website can check that they got exactly what the pipeline produced, nothing more and nothing less. And the manifest contains no numbers about the full database, because that stays private, too.

Why all this effort?

Because I’m lazy, in the good way. Arslantepe took many evenings. The next publication should take the evenings I need to check the data, not the evenings to build the machinery again. Now the machinery is there.

In the next part, I’ll show you where a release goes once it leaves the pipeline: the triplestore.

As always, if you have thoughts, suggestions, or your own story about getting data out of a research database, you know where to find me: info@lod-am.net or (if you have a GitHub account) in a comment below.

entry.title: Goals Reached - Looking Back at Where I Started
entry.content:
Hi again! Today is a good day for LOD-AM. When I started this sandbox back in June, I wrote down a list of goals on the About page. I didn’t really expect to tick them off this year, if ever. Well: we got there. Apart from a few last points in the automation workflow, every goal on that list is reached.

That deserves more than a single post. So here is a new series. In this first part I go through my old list, goal by goal. In the next parts I show you what happened behind the scenes in the last few days: the pipeline that turns my research database into Linked Data, the triplestore that is now open to everyone, and the website, where you can now query, search and cite the data yourself.

The list, goal by goal

Experiment with Linked Open Data for Ancient Metallurgy in a low-pressure sandbox. Check. And I mean experiment: my first prototype used a property that doesn’t even exist in CIDOC CRM 7.1.3 (I confessed that already). Failing was allowed, and I used that permission a lot.

Practice Learning by Doing. Check, with honours. I learned a whole lot about Eleventy, R2RML, SHACL, named graphs and some of the more elaborate features of Git(-hub). Some of it the hard way.

Build an RDF-based triple store to collect and combine archaeometallurgical data from diverse sources. Check. The triplestore is running, it holds the knowledge graph and the released data, and since today it is publicly queryable. "Diverse sources" is still a bit of a promise: so far, one publication is released, with the literature its chronologies come from. But the way from my research database to the triplestore now runs automatically, so the next publications are a question of checking, not of building.

Use blog posts as a public notebook, mistakes included. Check. This is post number eleven. Mistakes included, see above.

Display entities from the database directly on the site. Check. Every find, every analysis, every context, period and site has its own page under https://lod-am.net/id/. Start with the Data overview if you haven’t been there yet.

Keep it private and responsibility-free – for now, at least. Hmm. Half a check. LOD-AM is still my private one-person project, no institution behind it. But data with persistent IRIs, a public endpoint and a citation recommendation are a kind of responsibility. I’m fine with that. That’s what the sandbox was for.

Invite feedback and commentary. Always. My address is at the end of every post.

What’s left

A few last points in the automation workflow. Most of the chain from database to website runs on its own now, but some steps still need me on the server, and some small things need tidying. And honestly, that’s how it should be: the last step, putting data online, stays my decision. Every release arrives as a pull request, and I merge it.

As always, if you have thoughts, suggestions, or just want to celebrate a little with me, you know where to find me: info@lod-am.net or (if you have a GitHub account) in a comment below.

entry.title: Becoming Operational - Our Own Vocabularies, Linked to the AAT
entry.content:
So, back in The Vocabularies, I chose the Getty AAT for object and feature types, and Pleiades and PeriodO for sites and periods. I still stand by that choice. But the moment we started working with real data, I realised I needed something in between: local controlled vocabularies that say exactly what the sources say—and that are linked to the big vocabularies instead of being replaced by them.

Why not just use the AAT?

Here’s the thing: the AAT and an archaeometallurgical typology answer different questions. The AAT knows awls and chisels. It doesn’t know a Maykop fork or a single-bladed shaft-hole axe. If I simply replaced every type with the nearest AAT concept, I’d throw away exactly the information the typology was made for.

It’s the knife-or-scissors problem from my first data example all over again: the words we use for objects carry the judgement of the people who classified them. A vocabulary that’s too coarse silently overwrites that judgement.

The typology: built on SAM

For the object types, I didn’t start from scratch. The LOD-AM typology is based on the typology of the old SAM project (Studien zu den Anfängen der Metallurgie), as published by Krause in 2003, plus a few additions of my own:

Rüdiger Krause, Studien zur kupfer- und frühbronzezeitlichen Metallurgie zwischen Karpatenbecken und Ostsee (Rahden/Westf. 2003).

Why SAM? Because the SAM database will become one of the most important sources for LOD-AM. Its thousands of analyses of early metal objects are classified with exactly this typology. If LOD-AM speaks the same typological language, that data can come in without being forced into categories it was never meant for.

One might say, that I am not free of bias in regards to Rüdiger Krause. That's correct. I studied Vor- und Frühgeschichte in the Goethe University Frankfurt and I have been a student of his for many years. He did a lot to put me on the path, which let me to this point and I am deeply thankful for that and for many other things. So he more than earned this little citation.

The typology is a SKOS concept scheme with up to four levels. At the top are broad classes like daggers and other blades, axes and adzes or elements of dress and jewellery. Below them come type groups (daggers) and the types themselves (flat dagger or dagger, unspecified). Every concept has an English and a German label.

Connecting it to the AAT

Instead of replacing our types with AAT concepts, every concept that has a counterpart in the AAT is linked to it, with one of two SKOS relations:

  • skos:closeMatch when both mean (nearly) the same: our awl is a close match of AAT awls, our bowl of AAT bowls (vessels).
  • skos:broadMatch when the AAT concept is broader: our single-bladed shaft-hole axe has the broad match AAT axes (tools), our Maykop fork AAT forks (object genre).

Of the roughly 230 concepts in the typology, about a quarter are close matches, most others have a broad match, and only a handful (like unknown) have none. And yes—every single AAT identifier was checked against the Getty SPARQL endpoint. No invented IDs.

The best part? You can ask LOD-AM for "all daggers" in AAT terms and still get every object with the precise type the publication gave it. Global and local at the same time.

Site and feature types

The same idea works for sites and features. LOD-AM has its own small vocabulary of site and feature types—settlement, hoard, grave, kurgan, layer and a few more—each linked to the AAT where a fitting concept exists. Arslantepe is a settlement (close match: AAT settlements), the Palace Hoard a hoard (AAT hoards (groupings)), the Royal Tomb a grave (AAT graves).

Periods

For periods, I followed the way PeriodO organises them—and full transparency, after missing PeriodO’s hierarchies at first, I was glad to finally get this right. Every period belongs to the chronology system of its source. "Arslantepe VIA" always means Arslantepe VIA as defined there, with its own time-span (3350–3000 BC). The phases are grouped into cultures: Arslantepe VIA is a phase of the Northern Mesopotamian Late Chalcolithic, Arslantepe VIB1 of the Northern Mesopotamian Early Bronze Age. A context is dated to a phase; the culture follows from it.

What’s next: Pleiades and PeriodO

These local vocabularies aren’t the end point—they’re a bridge. Next, I’m going to connect them to the gazetteers I chose at the very beginning:

  • Sites will be linked to their Pleiades places. Where a site is still missing in Pleiades, I’ll add it.
  • Periods will go to PeriodO. Since our chronology systems are already organised the way PeriodO organises its collections, each of them can become one PeriodO collection.

Until then, the local vocabularies do their job: precise enough for the sources, and linked enough to be found.

Curious for the itty-bitty details?

View LOD-AM/knowledge-graph on GitHub →

As always, if you have thoughts, suggestions, or just want to talk vocabularies, you know where to find me: info@lod-am.net or (if you have a GitHub account) in a comment below.

entry.title: Becoming Operational - The Conventions
entry.content:
So, my first data example was written by hand, one triple at a time. That’s great for learning—but it doesn’t scale. As soon as you want to publish more than a handful of objects, you need rules. Rules that say exactly how an object, a site or an analysis is written down, and checks that refuse anything that breaks them.

That’s what the last weeks were about. All those rules now live in one place: the conventions of the knowledge graph. I won’t walk you through all of them here (that would be a very long and very boring post). Instead, here are three decisions that taught me something—and one confession.

The confession first

Remember when I wrote that crm:P71_is_listed_in might end up being one of the most frequent properties in the whole triple store? Well. It doesn’t even exist in CIDOC CRM 7.1.3. Neither did a few other things in my first prototype.

That’s why every term in LOD-AM is now checked automatically against the published ontologies—CIDOC CRM 7.1.3, CRMsci, CRMarchaeo, Allotrope and FaBiO—including whether a property is even allowed between the two things it connects. On top of that, the data is validated against SHACL shapes. If a term doesn’t exist, the data doesn’t go out. Publications are now linked with crm:P70i_is_documented_in, by the way.

1. We date the context, not the object

Here’s a question that sounds simple: how old is a dagger? In most publications, the honest answer is: we don’t know how old the dagger is. We know how old the grave is that it was found in.

So that’s what LOD-AM says. The object sits in its context—a grave, a hoard, a layer—using CRMarchaeo’s AP21i_is_contained_in, and only the context is dated: it witnessed a period (crm:P8i_witnessed). And if the grave lies in a kurgan, it’s part of the kurgan and of the site.

It’s a small shift, but it keeps the data honest. If someone redates the grave tomorrow, every object in it moves along—and nobody has to pretend we dated the objects themselves. Maybe that's something, only a prehistorian can say.

2. "Not detected" is not zero

This one hurts every archaeometallurgist who has ever worked with legacy tables. You open an old analysis table and find an empty cell. Or a dash. Or "n.d.". Or a 0. What do they mean? Was the element looked for and not found? Was it never measured? Was it below a detection limit nobody wrote down?

These are different statements, and LOD-AM keeps them apart:

  • a value below a stated limit ("< 0.001 %") is recorded as a maximum,
  • an element that was not analysed gets no measurement at all,
  • an element that was looked for but not detected gets a measurement without a value, marked as :not_detected:
:Bi_measurement a afr:AFR_0002099, crm:E54_Dimension ;   # mass fraction
    afx:AFX_0002816 chebi:33301 ;                       # quantifies bismuth atom
    crm:P2_has_type :not_detected ;
    qudt:unit unit:PERCENT .

And never, ever a 0. Which brings me to the most important rule of all: values are published as reported. Nothing is recalculated, normalised or rounded.

While I was at it, my AFO prototype got a proper overhaul too. The analysis now takes a sample, and a sampling event connects the sample to the object. Element contents are mass fractions (not concentrations), with real numbers and units instead of strings. And lead isotope ratios name both their isotopes.

3. Pleiades, but not "the same as"

In linked data, it’s tempting to say "our Arslantepe is the same as Pleiades’ Arslantepe" with owl:sameAs. Simple, done. But sameAs is a strong claim: it means everything Pleiades says about the place is now also true of our site, and everything we say is true of theirs. Merge two datasets with slightly different ideas of a site, and you get a mess.

So when a site is linked to Pleiades, the Pleiades URI becomes an identifier of our site—a pointer, not a merger. Next to it, the site keeps the name as reported in the publication, because that name is the link back to the literature, and a real GeoSPARQL geometry, so a triple store can actually do spatial queries with it.

Everything else

There’s more: one IRI per record under https://lod-am.net/id/, labels in English and German, our own typology for object types (that one gets the next post), and a bibliography that comes straight from my public Zotero group. Curious for the itty-bitty details?

Read CONVENTIONS.md on GitHub →

Why all this effort?

Because the next step was real data. With the conventions in place and every rule checked automatically, a dataset is no longer something I craft by hand—it’s something that has to pass. In the last post of this series, I’ll show you the first one that did.

As always, if you have thoughts, suggestions, or just want to geek out about data modelling, you know where to find me: info@lod-am.net or (if you have a GitHub account) in a comment below.

entry.title: Becoming Operational - Why I Switched from Mistral to Claude
entry.content:
Hi again! It’s been quiet on the blog for a while—but not in the repositories. A lot happened, and over the next few posts I’ll tell you how LOD-AM went from a hand-written example to its first real dataset online. But before I get to that, there’s something I want to get out of the way. I promised to be transparent about how this project is built, so here it is: I changed my AI assistant.

From Mistral to Claude

In How I started, I wrote that this website was pretty much a vibe coding attempt with Mistral. That was true back then. Since then, LOD-AM has been built with Claude, Anthropic’s AI assistant, working directly in my GitHub repositories.

I am glad enough to work with a lot of colleagues, who love to experiment with every piece of technology available. And when I got a recommendation and a report of his recent progress from my dear colleague Lasse, I just had to try it out. We'll see how the European competitors of Anthropic will do. I am hoping for the best. Competition boosts business afterall.

Why? Time.

Here’s the thing: LOD-AM is a free-time project. It has to fit into spare evenings between everything else. Every hour I spend on it has to count—so I have to be as effective as possible. And with Claude, I simply get more done.

What made the difference for me isn’t that Claude can write code. It’s that it can carry a task from start to finish: read my conventions, change the data model, run the checks, look at the result in a browser, and come back with a pull request I can review. And when something fails, it tells me what failed—instead of pretending it worked.

Who decides what?

This part matters most to me, so let me be clear about it:

The research decisions are mine. What a value in a publication means, which type an object belongs to, which period a context dates to—whenever something is a domain judgement and not a fact from a specification, Claude doesn’t decide it. It writes the question down, and I answer it. My sandbox, still my rules.

Claude does the heavy lifting. Writing and testing the conversion, looking up ontology terms, checking every AAT identifier against the Getty endpoint, building the pages you see here, keeping the documentation up to date.

Nothing goes live without me. Claude works on branches and opens pull requests. I review them, and I merge them.

Trust, but check

There’s one mistake an AI assistant makes all too easily in a project like this: inventing an ontology term that looks perfectly plausible but doesn’t exist. That’s why every single term in LOD-AM is now checked automatically against the published ontologies before anything is merged. I don’t have to trust the assistant—I can check it.

And these posts?

Full transparency here as well: Claude drafted this series from our notes, issues and pull requests. I went through it, changed what didn’t sound like me, and I stand behind every word.

Curious how the rules for Claude look? They’re in the repositories, right next to the code:

View LOD-AM/knowledge-graph on GitHub →

As always, if you have thoughts, suggestions, or just want to talk about working with AI in research, you know where to find me: info@lod-am.net or (if you have a GitHub account) in a comment below.

entry.title: Becoming Operational - Arslantepe Is Online
entry.content:
This is the post I’ve been waiting to write since the very beginning of LOD-AM: the first complete dataset is online! Every find and every analysis from Arslantepe published by Hauptmann, Schmitt-Strecker, Begemann and Palmieri in 2002 is now available as Linked Open Data—right here on this website, one page per record.

Chemical Composition and Lead Isotopy of Metal Objects from the "Royal" Tomb and Other Related Finds at Arslantepe, Eastern Anatoliadoi.org

Back to where it started

Arslantepe has been with LOD-AM from the start. Back in July, I picked this very paper as my test case—because it throws pretty much every modelling problem of legacy data at you: fragments without types, one artifact with two samples, "not detected" values, and three different ID systems. It was a minefield. Now it’s no longer a test case. It’s the real thing.

What’s in it

We collected the Arslantepe data directly from the publication and modelled it following the conventions and vocabularies from this series. Here’s what you get:

  • 58 finds (metal objects and casting waste), each with its type from the LOD-AM typology, linked to the Getty AAT;
  • 78 analyses: 50 chemical analyses with 14 elements each, and 28 lead isotope analyses by the Deutsches Bergbau-Museum Bochum with three lead isotope ratios each;
  • 7 archaeological contexts, among them the famous Royal Tomb with 38 of the finds, and the Palace Hoard;
  • the periods they date to, from Arslantepe VII to VIC, each with its time-span and its culture.

And every value is exactly as the publication reported it. Where an element was looked for but not found, the data says "not detected"—not 0. Nothing is recalculated.

Where to find it

  • The Data overview, with lists of all finds, analyses, contexts, periods and more.
  • The Arslantepe site page, the Royal Tomb and the Palace Hoard.
  • The publication page, which brings all records of the article together.
  • And the whole dataset as RDF (Turtle) for download, under CC BY 4.0.

Every record has its own IRI under https://lod-am.net/id/. So you can cite and link a single find or a single analysis—not just the article.

A word of thanks

I’m really proud of this one. Getting here meant many evenings of checking types, contexts, periods and values, and deciding, again and again, what the publication actually says. And I have to say it: I’m impressed by Claude’s performance along the way. It turned my decisions into a data model, a conversion and these pages, it caught inconsistencies I would have overlooked, and it never got tired of yet another round of checks. For a free-time project like mine, that made all the difference. But enough, that already sounds like advertisement, but it really worked....

This is only the beginning

Arslantepe is the first dataset—but it won’t stay alone for long. The conventions, the vocabularies and the checks are in place now, and they work. That’s why I’m sure we’ll make more data from many more publications available soon.

Curious for the code behind the pages?

View LOD-AM/website on GitHub →

As always, if you have thoughts, suggestions, or find something in the data that doesn’t look right, you know where to find me: info@lod-am.net or (if you have a GitHub account) in a comment below.

entry.title: Learning by Doing
entry.content:
It’s been a while since my last post. That’s just how these learning-by-doing projects go, especially when you’re fitting them into spare moments between everything else. But I haven’t been idle. Far from it. I’ve been working on turning my ontological ideas into actual data—and I’m ready to share the first example.

You can find the itty-bitty details here: https://github.com/LOD-AM/ontologies/blob/main/examples/lod-am-example.ttl

View LOD-AM/ontologies on GitHub →

Sticking Closer to CIDOC-CRM Than Expected

If you’ve been following along, you know I’m not the biggest fan of event-based modeling. But here’s the thing about good research: sometimes you have to follow the logic, even when it takes you somewhere you didn’t expect. In this case, that somewhere was closer to vanilla CIDOC-CRM than I originally planned.

Now, I didn’t go all-in on events. I still avoided modeling excavation events, collection histories, or legal provenance. Not because those aren’t important—they absolutely are—but because they’re not my focus. There are better specialists and better projects out there for those questions. My sandbox, my rules.

Where I Kept the Events

There are a few places where I did embrace the event-based approach, and for good reason.

Typological Assignments: At first glance, it’s tempting to just say:

:object1 crm:P2_has_type :spearhead .

Simple, straightforward, queryable. But here’s the catch: typology isn’t always black and white. Different regions use different terminologies. Even within the same system, the same artifact might be a knife to one researcher and a dagger to another—and both could be right.

I learned this the hard way during my very first Hiwi job at university. I was entering thousands of paper records into a database for an Iron Age site in southern Germany. At some point, we realized we’d duplicated some iron finds. As I worked through the deduplication, I noticed something interesting: the same artifact might be recorded as a knife in one document and as half of a pair of scissors in another. There’s only one physical truth, but typologically, both classifications can be valid.

So, I decided to stick with CIDOC’s approach. Every typological assignment now lives in its own crm:E17_Type_Assignment entity, with its own context. Same goes for crm:E4_Period assignments—I’m keeping each dating in its own crm:E52_Time-Span node.

The AFO Prototype

I’ve also got a prototype running for the Allotrope Framework. Every analyzed object is defined as afm:AFM_0001099 (an object of mixed chemical composition in AFO-speak). That’s where the ontologies overlap.

For the analysis itself, AFO offers some handy classes. Spectrometry, for example, uses afp:AFP_0000527. And for results, AFO has properties for absolute and relative values. An absolute value might look like this:

:Ag_measurement a afr:AFR_0002036 ;
    afx:AFX_0002816 chebi:23855 ;  # Silver
    afo:value "0.002"^^xsd:decimal ;
    afo:unit "PERCENT" .

And a relative value (like a maximum or minimum) would use a different property:

:Pb_measurement a afr:AFR_0002036 ;
    afx:AFX_0002816 chebi:28702 ;  # Lead
    afx:AFX_0000331 "0.001"^^xsd:decimal ;  # <0.001%
    afo:unit "PERCENT" .

Here, chebi (Chemical Entities of Biological Interest) acts as a controlled vocabulary for the elements.

I was lucky enough to get into contact with some AFO specialists from NFDI4Chem. We will see, how my first prototype will hold up to their judgment. In any case, I am sure, that I am going to learn a lot from that.

FABIO

As for literature, I didn’t reinvent the wheel. FABIO is a well-established standard, and I implemented it pretty much as-is. The connection point to CIDOC is usually crm:P71_is_listed_in—which might end up being one of the most frequent properties in the whole triple store.

What’s Next?

So, what’s on the horizon? A few things, not necessarily in this order:

First, I just got an account with Pleiades. They’ve been incredibly responsive—Tom Elliott even spread the word about my little project. Tom, if you’re reading this: Thank you! I’m looking forward to sharing my experiences with Pleiades soon.

I’m also planning to produce PeriodO-aligned data. Full transparency: I initially missed that PeriodO does support hierarchical relationships between periods. Turns out I just picked unlucky test cases at first. Now that I see it, I’m excited to dive in.

And, because I’m all about efficiency, I’m working on some automation—generating my own data from CSV files and pulling terms from Getty AAT into my triple store.

So, that’s where things stand. Still learning, still building, still figuring it out as I go. And as always, if you have thoughts, suggestions, or just want to geek out about data modeling, you know where to find me: info@lod-am.net or (if you have a GitHub account) in a comment below.

entry.title: Tackling Legacy Data practically
entry.content:
So, I’ve got my ontologies sorted and my vocabularies in place. But none of that matters much if I don’t have real data to work with. That’s where this 2002 paper comes in.

Curious for the paper itself?

Chemical Composition and Lead Isotopy of Metal Objects from the "Royal" Tomb and Other Related Finds at Arslantepe, Eastern Anatoliadoi.org

Why This Paper?

Here’s the thing: I needed a real-world example that exposes the messy, complicated data issues we face in archaeometallurgy. And this paper by Hauptmann, Schmitt-Strecker, Begemann, and Palmieri is perfect.

Arslantepe—a 30-meter-high tell in Eastern Anatolia—has a "Royal Tomb" complex from the Early Bronze Age, packed with objects made from alloys that have been analyzed for both trace elements and lead isotopes. It’s a goldmine of data, but it’s also a minefield of modelling challenges.

The Six Challenges It Throws At Us

Working through this paper, I quickly realized it forces me to confront six critical modelling questions that keep coming up in legacy archaeometallurgical literature:

1. The Unknowns: Fragments Without Types

So, there are metal fragments in the assemblage that can’t be assigned a definitive typology. They’re just... fragments. No clear morphology, no easy classification. This is a fundamental issue in archaeology: how do you represent objects when you don’t have enough information to classify them? It’s not just about missing data—it’s about structural uncertainty in your knowledge model. If we can’t handle unknowns gracefully, we can’t model real-world archaeology.

2. The Double Analysis: Trace Elements + Lead Isotopes

The paper presents both trace element compositions and lead isotope ratios for the same artifacts. This isn’t just about storing two datasets—it’s about linking analytical methods that tell different stories. Trace elements speak to alloy composition and technological choices; lead isotopes reveal provenance and trade networks. The challenge? Modelling these as complementary but distinct lines of evidence that together tell a richer story about the object’s history.

3. The Chronology Puzzle: Multiple Complexes, Different Dates

Arslantepe’s Royal Tomb and Palace hoard belong to different archaeological complexes with distinct chronological attributions. This is where stratigraphic reality meets data modelling: sites don’t have single dates, they have complex temporal layers. The question is how to represent objects that belong to different phases, with different dating methods, and sometimes overlapping timeframes—without flattening the archaeological record into oversimplified categories.

4. The Fuzzy Data: ">0.1%", "<0.5%", "Not Detected"

The paper includes qualitative descriptors like ">0.1%", ">0.5%", or "not detected" rather than precise values. This is real analytical data—not sloppy work, but the nature of detection limits and measurement uncertainty. The modelling challenge is preserving this nuance while still making the data queryable. If we force everything into exact numbers, we lose the honesty of the original analysis. If we treat it as text, we lose the ability to reason computationally.

5. The Spearhead Problem: One Artifact, Two Samples

Two samples were taken from different parts of the same spearhead—one from the blade, one from the socket—yielding different results. This exposes a fundamental tension in archaeometallurgical data: the artifact (the conceptual whole) vs. the sample (the physical fragment analyzed). How do we maintain the relationship between them? How do we track that sample A and sample B come from the same object, but represent different materials or manufacturing processes? Get this wrong, and you lose the very connections that make the data meaningful.

6. The ID Chaos: Excavation, Lab, and Publication Systems

The artifacts carry three different identifier schemes from different contexts. This is the reality of legacy data integration: every institution, every project, every publication creates its own system. The challenge isn’t just technical—it’s conceptual. How do we reconcile that "Tomb 16/H/50" in the excavation log, "AR-23" in the lab notebook, and "Fig. 3, no. 12" in the paper all refer to the same physical object? Without solving this, we can’t link datasets, and without linking datasets, we can’t do meaningful cross-project research.

The Roadmap: From Paper to Queryable Data

So here’s my plan: over the next series of posts, I’ll tackle each challenge systematically.

Next Post: Modelling Unknowns: Fragments, Fuzzy Values, and Probabilistic Typing

  • Deep dive into CIDOC-CRM + Getty AAT for uncertain classifications
  • Implementing a lean apllication of CIDOC-CRM for the given use-case.

Following Post: The Analytical Workflow: Linking Trace Elements and Lead Isotopes with AFO

  • Step-by-step mapping of measurements (fuzzy or not) based on AFO

Later Post: Temporal Modelling: Arslantepe’s Stratigraphy in PeriodO

  • How I extended PeriodO with local phases
  • Experimenting with a hierarchy for chronological phases

Final Post: The Full Arslantepe Dataset: Querying the Triple Store

  • Live SPARQL endpoint demonstration
  • Example queries addressing all six challenges

As always, if you have thoughts, suggestions, or just want to nerd out about archaeometallurgical data modelling, write me an Email to info@lod-am.net or (if you have a GitHub account) in a comment below.
